name: Alyona and towers
description: Alyona has built n towers by putting small cubes some on the top of others. Each cube has size 1 × 1 × 1 . A tower is a non-zero amount of cubes standing on the top of each other. The towers are next to each other, forming a row. Sometimes Alyona chooses some segment towers, and put on the top of each tower several cubes. Formally, Alyouna chooses some segment of towers from l i to r i and adds d i cubes on the top of them. Let the sequence a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n be the heights of the towers from left to right. Let's call as a segment of towers a l , a l + 1 , ..., a r a hill if the following condition holds: there is integer k ( l ≤ k ≤ r ) such that a l < a l + 1 < a l + 2 < ... < a k > a k + 1 > a k + 2 > ... > a r . After each addition of d i cubes on the top of the towers from l i to r i , Alyona wants to know the maximum width among all hills. The width of a hill is the number of towers in it.
input_specification: The first line contain single integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 3·10 5 ) — the number of towers. The second line contain n integers a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n ( 1 ≤ a i ≤ 10 9 ) — the number of cubes in each tower. The third line contain single integer m ( 1 ≤ m ≤ 3·10 5 ) — the number of additions. The next m lines contain 3 integers each. The i -th of these lines contains integers l i , r i and d i ( 1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n , 1 ≤ d i ≤ 10 9 ), that mean that Alyona puts d i cubes on the tio of each of the towers from l i to r i .
output_specification: Print m lines. In i -th line print the maximum width of the hills after the i -th addition.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 739C — Alyona and towers [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
